title: Pooled or straight-line? How your Florida condo's reserve money is counted, in plain words
seoTitle: Florida Condo Pooled vs. Straight-Line Reserves
description: Florida condo reserves can be straight-line or pooled. What each means, a simple example, the SIRS pooling limit, and what to ask before the board switches.
dek: Two words on your budget decide how the savings for the roof, the windows and the structure are counted. Here is what straight-line and pooled reserves mean, with a simple example, and what Florida law says about switching.
facebook: Your condo budget says "pooled" or "straight-line" next to the reserves. Ever wonder what that means for your monthly bill? Here's a plain-words explainer with a simple example, plus a state rule change open for comment until Nov. 12.
keywords: pooled vs straight-line reserves Florida condo
can condo board switch to pooled reserves without a vote

body.text: Budget season is here, and many Florida condo owners are looking at a reserve schedule for the first time. Next to the numbers, you may see one of two words: "straight-line" or "pooled." They also shape how much goes into savings each year, and how easily that money can be used when a big bill comes.

This article explains both methods, walks through a simple made-up example, and lays out what Florida law says. It is a guide, not legal advice. For your building, the association attorney and the person who prepared your reserve study are the right people to ask.

body.title: Terms to know
body.text: Reserves: money the association sets aside for big future repairs and replacements, like the roof. Component: one item the association saves for, such as the roof or the windows. Remaining useful life: how many years an item is expected to last from now. SIRS: the structural integrity reserve study, required at least every 10 years for condo buildings three habitable stories or higher. It covers the roof, the structure, fireproofing and fire protection, plumbing, electrical, waterproofing and exterior painting, windows and exterior doors, and certain other costly items tied to them.
What Florida law requires either way

Section 718.112(2)(f) of the 2026 Florida Statutes says the budget must include reserve accounts for capital expenditures and deferred maintenance. Those accounts must include roof replacement, building painting, pavement resurfacing, and any other item whose deferred maintenance expense or replacement cost is more than $25,000, a figure the state adjusts each year for inflation.

The law says the amount to be reserved must be computed with a formula based on each item's estimated remaining useful life and estimated replacement cost or deferred maintenance expense. Straight-line and pooled are two ways of doing that math.
Straight-line: one savings jar per item

With straight-line reserves, the association keeps a separate reserve account for each item. A November 2025 newspaper column by Becker & Poliakoff attorney Joseph E. Adams describes the math this way: take the item's estimated cost, subtract what is already saved for it, and divide by the years it has left. If an account is short, the shortfall is added to that year's amount.
Here is a made-up example. Real buildings will have different numbers.

items: Roof: costs $300,000 to replace, $100,000 already saved, 10 years left. ($300,000 minus $100,000) divided by 10 is $20,000 a year.
Windows and exterior doors: cost $200,000, $50,000 already saved, 15 years left. ($200,000 minus $50,000) divided by 15 is $10,000 a year.
Straight-line total for these two items: $30,000 a year, kept in two separate jars.

body.text: The upside is clarity. Every owner can see exactly what is saved for each item. The downside, as a Palm Beach Post column by attorney Ryan Poliakoff puts it, is that money can be sitting in the wrong jar. If the roof comes due early, the window money is not meant to help, and the board may need extra money from owners even though the reserves overall have cash.
Pooled: one savings jar for several items

With pooled reserves, two or more items share one account. The Adams column describes the goal: the money on hand, plus what the association plans to add each year, must be at least enough to pay the projected costs of all the pooled items as they come due.

In our example, the roof and windows would share one jar. The yearly deposit is not simply $20,000 plus $10,000. Instead, the reserve study preparer builds a year-by-year schedule of money in and money out, and sets deposits so the pool never runs short. The answer can be higher or lower than the straight-line total, depending on when each item is due.

Florida law puts limits on pooling. Section 718.112(2)(f)4 says the items covered by the SIRS may only be pooled with other SIRS items. So a roof and windows can share a pool, but pavement resurfacing, which is not a SIRS item, cannot go in that same pool. The statute also says the budgeted funding for a pool must be enough that available funds meet or exceed projected expenses, measured against the reserve funding plan in the building's most recent SIRS.
Can the board switch methods without a vote?
The statute says a vote of the members is not required for the board to change the accounting method for reserves to a pooling or straight-line method. But that is not the whole story.

items: For buildings that need a SIRS, budgets adopted on or after December 31, 2024 may not provide less in reserves for SIRS items than the law requires, even with an owner vote.
Reserve money must stay in the reserve accounts. Associations that need a SIRS may not vote to use SIRS reserve money for any other purpose.

The Poliakoff column says the long-held view among lawyers is that money already collected under straight-line could not be moved into a pool without an owner vote, and that the statute's wording is unclear.

The state rule that explains reserves, Rule 61B-22.005 of the Florida Administrative Code, was updated effective October 4, 2026. On October 22, 2026, the Division of Florida Condominiums, Timeshares and Mobile Homes proposed another change to clarify switching between pooled and straight-line accounting and adjustments to yearly reserve funding.

body.text: The October 22 proposal's public comment period on flrules.org runs through November 12, 2026. Comments sent through the site must be 8,000 characters or less. A proposed rule is not in force until it is adopted.
What to do
If you are an owner:

items: Find the word "pooled" or "straight-line" on your proposed budget's reserve schedule. If it is not there, ask the board in writing which method is used.
If the reserves are pooled, ask whether SIRS items are in a separate pool from non-SIRS items like paving.
If the board plans to switch methods, ask what the association attorney said, and whether money already saved will be moved.
Want to weigh in on the proposed rule change? Search "61B-22.005" on flrules.org and use the comment link before November 12.

body.text: If you serve on the board:

items: Ask your reserve study preparer to show the reserve funding for the coming year both ways, so the board and owners can see the difference.
Have the association attorney read Rule 61B-22.005, as updated October 4, before any change in method.
Explain the method in plain words in the budget packet, so owners know what they are paying for.
Watch the October 22 proposal. If it is adopted, the rules on switching may change again. DBPR's condo division can answer process questions.

faq.q: What is the difference between pooled and straight-line reserves?
faq.a: Straight-line keeps a separate reserve account for each item, like the roof or the windows, funded by its cost minus what is saved, divided by the years left. Pooled puts two or more items in one account, funded so the money on hand plus planned deposits covers all the pooled items' costs as they come due.

faq.q: Can a Florida condo board switch to pooled reserves without an owner vote?
faq.a: Section 718.112(2)(f)4 of the Florida Statutes says no member vote is required to change the reserve accounting method. The state reserve rule, 61B-22.005, was updated October 4, 2026, and another change about switching was proposed October 22. Ask the association attorney before any switch.

faq.q: Can SIRS reserves be pooled with other reserves in Florida?
faq.a: Only with other SIRS items. The statute says reserve funding for SIRS components, such as the roof, structure, plumbing, electrical, waterproofing and windows, may only be pooled with other SIRS components.

faq.q: Is pooled reserve funding cheaper for condo owners?
faq.a: Not always. The yearly amount for a pool comes from a year-by-year cash schedule in the reserve study, so it can be higher or lower than the straight-line total depending on when items come due. Ask your reserve study preparer to show both.

faq.q: How do I comment on Florida's proposed condo reserve rule change?
faq.a: The proposed change to Rule 61B-22.005 was published October 22, 2026. Its comment period on flrules.org runs through November 12, 2026. Search the rule number on flrules.org and use the comment link; comments there are limited to 8,000 characters.
